title: When the Interval Is Smaller Than the Instrument: code and analysis for two failure modes of streaming latency benchmarks

creators.name: Ricou, Gustavo Pedro
creators.affiliation: School of Computer Science and Statistics, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland

description:
Code, analysis and manuscript for a study of two failure modes of sub-millisecond streaming latency benchmarking, both governed by one ratio: the instrument's timescale over the interval being measured.

Mode A (inversion): cross-process latency is a two-clock difference and cannot be negative; applied to every run, that check rejected 1,321 of 2,266, including every run behind a statistically clean result we were about to publish. The mechanism is scheduling, not clock skew, established by manipulation: real-time priority on the stamping threads collapses the inversion rate by 39x and 54x at fixed utilisation, and two core geometries at identical utilisation differ by 2.07x.

Mode B (deletion): the OpenMessaging Benchmark silently deletes every sample whose millisecond-quantised difference is not positive. Across 223 instrumented runs it computed its reported distribution from 0.36% to 100% of the samples it took, reporting the same median either way. Retention obeys a grid law in the reduced fraction of send interval over timestamp quantum, confirmed by a pre-registered payload manipulation, reproduced by a 200-line Python harness with no JVM, and measured across two clocks. The sign channel caught 41,403 genuine one-tick causality violations being absorbed by the same guard.

What changed in v2.6. Fourteen further rounds of adversarial internal review, all of them on the presentation and the provenance rather than on the science: no result, estimate or interval in this release differs from v2.5. The substantive changes: (1) A figure for Mode B's mechanism — the earlier figures showed that the deletion law holds and none drew the geometry that produces it: one delivery at four phases of a tick, three of them measuring exactly zero, beside the phase set a commensurate producer actually visits. (2) Every quantity the manuscript prints is now emitted from the committed artefacts. Round 34 found the payload sweep's endpoints typed in twenty places across the two documents and the figure scripts — every copy correct, which is why none had ever failed — and round 38 found the last typed range. (3) Eight new gates, each demonstrated failing on the defect it guards before that defect was repaired: subsection numbering and pointer resolution, placement claims between the two documents, ordinal claims against the emitted ranking, table-caption conventions, figure-to-ledger agreement, a rule that code may not cite the manuscript by number (which retired twenty-six unresolvable citations, seventeen of them in the arabic numbering the paper abandoned at the TC restructure — one of those was drawn into a published supplement figure), printed ranges that must be read from the ledger rather than typed, and the bolded claim that opens a figure caption. (4) Terminology: retention is defined where the paper defines its other terms, because in the Kafka ecosystem the word already means log-retention time. The test suite is now 3,650 tests at 100% branch coverage, up from 2,501.

The archive contains the instrumentation, every campaign script and ledger, the analysis suite that recomputes the manuscript's numbers from committed data and fails if paper and data disagree, the manuscript, and its supplement. A SHA256SUMS manifest lists every file in the archive so any single file can be verified independently of the zip.

Data note. No StatsBomb event data is redistributed. Replay plans derived from it are excluded from this record and regenerable byte-for-byte from a pinned upstream commit with the included scripts.
